nameStory: The disc gyro gets its name from its flat, disc-like shell that spins like a tiny gyroscope when disturbed in the water. The word 'gyro' comes from the Greek word for 'circle' or 'ring,' perfectly describing this snail's coiled, flattened spiral shell that looks like nature's own spinning top.
description: The disc gyro is a tiny freshwater snail with a flat, tightly coiled shell that rarely exceeds a quarter-inch across. Unlike the tall, pointed shells of many snails, this little mollusk's shell is compressed into an almost perfectly flat spiral, resembling a miniature brown or tan coin. It glides along underwater surfaces using its muscular foot, feeding on algae and tiny organic particles. These small aquatic snails are part of the ramshorn snail family, known for their distinctive coiled shells.

idTips.label: Flat spiral shell
idTips.description: Shell is extremely flattened, almost disc-like, with tight coils that lie nearly in the same plane - feels smooth and firm like a tiny flat button

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically less than 6mm (about 1/4 inch) across - roughly the size of a pencil eraser or small peppercorn

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell ranges from pale tan to light brown, sometimes with a slightly translucent quality that shows the internal whorls

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Shell surface is smooth to the touch with fine growth lines visible, lacking the ridges or spines found on some other freshwater snails

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along submerged surfaces, often rotating or spinning when disturbed, creating the gyroscope effect that gives it its name

habitat: Look for disc gyros in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and the shallow edges of lakes throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant aquatic vegetation and soft substrates where algae and organic matter accumulate. You'll often find them crawling on submerged plants, rocks, or the muddy bottom in water less than a few feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, beginning to feed and reproduce. Look for them on emerging aquatic vegetation and along shallow, sun-warmed shorelines.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during warm months. They're frequently visible grazing on algae-covered surfaces and aquatic plants in shallow water.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water as temperatures cool. Continue feeding to build energy reserves for winter.
seasonality.winter: Become less active and may burrow into soft sediments or remain inactive under ice. Rarely observed during coldest months.

funFact: Despite being so small you could fit dozens on a quarter, disc gyros are actually important ecosystem engineers that help keep freshwater environments clean by constantly grazing on algae and breaking down organic matter into nutrients that feed the entire aquatic food web.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small ramshorn snails, but the disc gyro's extremely flattened shell sets it apart - if it looks like someone stepped on a regular spiral snail and flattened it into a disc, you've probably found a disc gyro.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'gyro,' this has nothing to do with the Greek food - both get their names from the same Greek root meaning 'circle.' The ramshorn snail family name comes from their resemblance to the curved horns of a ram when viewed from the side.
compareHints: The disc gyro can be distinguished from its relative, the flexed gyro, by its more consistently flat profile and tighter coiling pattern. While both are small ramshorn snails, the flexed gyro tends to have a slightly more raised or deflected shell shape, whereas the disc gyro maintains its characteristically flat, coin-like appearance. The disc gyro's shell also tends to be more symmetrical and evenly coiled compared to other gyro snails.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative the disc gyro, the flexed gyro is smaller and has a more tightly wound, flatter spiral shell.
